messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Marcus had always been the kind of person who managed things quietly and efficiently — the one in the server room at 2 a.m. when a database crashed, methodical and calm under pressure. At thirty-five, he had built a life around predictability: clean data structures, scheduled backups, controlled outcomes. Then, in the winter of that year, he developed what he initially dismissed as a persistent chest infection. By the time he was admitted to the emergency department, his oxygen saturation had dropped dangerously low, and he was diagnosed with a severe bilateral pneumonia that progressed rapidly to respiratory failure. For eleven days he lay in an ICU bed, a nasal cannula replaced by a non-rebreather mask, then by high-flow oxygen. He watched nurses adjust IV drips above his arm, felt the cold slide of a needle each time a blood draw was ordered, and endured the particular helplessness of not being able to draw a full breath while clinicians leaned over him with stethoscopes and pulse oximeters. His then-wife, sitting beside him on the third day, had been told quietly in the corridor that the situation was serious. Marcus had heard enough of that conversation to understand what serious meant.

He was discharged six weeks later, lungs scarred but functional. In the months that followed, the world did not feel the way it had before. His body, which had once been a neutral instrument he relied on without thinking, had become something he monitored constantly. He was certain, in a way he could not argue himself out of, that it would fail him again without warning, and that next time there would be no recovery. What frightened him most was not death in the abstract but the specific sensation of breathlessness — the memory of that suffocating tightness lived somewhere beneath conscious thought, and any hint of it in his chest now sent a wave of fear through him that felt indistinguishable from the original emergency. He had come to believe that a racing heart or tightening lungs were not normal fluctuations but early signals of catastrophe.

Over the following year, Marcus reorganised his life around managing these signals. He stopped exercising entirely, convinced that the exertion would bring on the breathlessness he dreaded. He began restricting what he ate, monitoring his diet with the same granular attention he brought to database queries, finding that the sense of control over intake was one of the few things that quieted the background hum of physical unease. He cancelled a routine dental appointment, then a follow-up with his pulmonologist, then another. Hospitals, ambulances glimpsed from the road, even the antiseptic smell of a pharmacy — all of it had become intolerable. He rerouted his commute to avoid the street where the hospital stood.

At work, where he spent long hours alone in front of screens, the avoidance was easier to maintain. But the cost accumulated. His divorce, finalised eight months after his discharge, had been shaped in part by his withdrawal — his ex-wife had described living with someone who had become unreachable, sealed off. He had not contested her characterisation. Colleagues noticed that he declined team lunches and avoided the office first-aid room, once leaving a meeting abruptly when a colleague mentioned a recent surgery. His manager had begun asking questions.

When Marcus finally sought help, it was because of a moment at his desk. A routine system alert had caused his screen to flash red — the same colour as the low-oxygen warning light he remembered from the ICU monitor — and he had found himself unable to breathe properly for nearly twenty minutes, hands gripping the edge of his keyboard, certain something was happening to him. A colleague had called building security. The incident left him humiliated and shaken in equal measure.

He arrived at the intake appointment guarded and precise in his language, as though clinical accuracy might create some distance from the material. He said he was not sure therapy could help with something that felt so physical. What he was most afraid of, he admitted after a long pause, was that he would spend the rest of his life waiting for his body to betray him again. What he hoped for, more quietly, was to stop.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Negative Emotions: The vignette focuses primarily on fear but does not clearly reflect the broader range of strong negative emotions reported by the patient, such as horror, anger, guilt, or shame.: The patient self-reported experiencing strong negative feelings including fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame (Negative Emotions item). While fear is well-represented throughout the vignette, the other emotions in this cluster — horror, anger, guilt, and shame — are largely absent. Humiliation is briefly mentioned at the end, but this is situational and does not capture the broader persistent emotional profile the patient endorsed. A clinical paraphrase acknowledging at least some of these other affective states (e.g., a sense of shame about his condition, anger at his body's betrayal, or horror at the ICU experience) would be needed to fully reflect this item.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Marcus had always been the kind of person who managed things quietly and efficiently — the one in the server room at 2 a.m. when a database crashed, methodical and calm under pressure. At thirty-five, he had built a life around predictability: clean data structures, scheduled backups, controlled outcomes. Then, in the winter of that year, he developed what he initially dismissed as a persistent chest infection. By the time he was admitted to the emergency department, his oxygen saturation had dropped dangerously low, and he was diagnosed with a severe bilateral pneumonia that progressed rapidly to respiratory failure. For eleven days he lay in an ICU bed, a nasal cannula replaced by a non-rebreather mask, then by high-flow oxygen. He watched nurses adjust IV drips above his arm, felt the cold slide of a needle each time a blood draw was ordered, and endured the particular helplessness of not being able to draw a full breath while clinicians leaned over him with stethoscopes and pulse oximeters. His then-wife, sitting beside him on the third day, had been told quietly in the corridor that the situation was serious. Marcus had heard enough of that conversation to understand what serious meant. What stayed with him from those eleven days was not any single moment but a texture of sustained horror — the low-oxygen warning light casting its red pulse across the ceiling, the mechanical rhythm of the oxygen equipment, the knowledge that his body was doing something he could not stop or negotiate with.

He was discharged six weeks later, lungs scarred but functional. In the months that followed, the world did not feel the way it had before. His body, which had once been a neutral instrument he relied on without thinking, had become something he monitored constantly. He was certain, in a way he could not argue himself out of, that it would fail him again without warning, and that next time there would be no recovery. What frightened him most was not death in the abstract but the specific sensation of breathlessness — the memory of that suffocating tightness lived somewhere beneath conscious thought, and any hint of it in his chest now sent a wave of fear through him that felt indistinguishable from the original emergency. He had come to believe that a racing heart or tightening lungs were not normal fluctuations but early signals of catastrophe. Alongside the fear ran something darker and less manageable: a low, persistent anger at his own body, at the sheer arbitrariness of what had happened to him. He had done nothing wrong. He had been healthy, careful, unremarkable in his habits — and still his lungs had simply stopped working. That felt, in some register he could not fully articulate, like a betrayal he had not deserved and could not forgive. There was shame in it too, a corrosive kind — shame at having been reduced to helplessness in front of his wife, at having needed strangers to manage his most basic functions, at the fact that he could not simply recover and move on the way he felt he should have been able to.

Over the following year, Marcus reorganised his life around managing these signals. He stopped exercising entirely, convinced that the exertion would bring on the breathlessness he dreaded. He began restricting what he ate, monitoring his diet with the same granular attention he brought to database queries, finding that the sense of control over intake was one of the few things that quieted the background hum of physical unease. He cancelled a routine dental appointment, then a follow-up with his pulmonologist, then another. Hospitals, ambulances glimpsed from the road, even the antiseptic smell of a pharmacy — all of it had become intolerable. He rerouted his commute to avoid the street where the hospital stood.

At work, where he spent long hours alone in front of screens, the avoidance was easier to maintain. But the cost accumulated. His divorce, finalised eight months after his discharge, had been shaped in part by his withdrawal — his ex-wife had described living with someone who had become unreachable, sealed off. He had not contested her characterisation, though privately he felt a guilt about it that he had no idea what to do with — a sense that his inability to recover properly had cost her something she had not signed up to lose. Colleagues noticed that he declined team lunches and avoided the office first-aid room, once leaving a meeting abruptly when a colleague mentioned a recent surgery. His manager had begun asking questions.

When Marcus finally sought help, it was because of a moment at his desk. A routine system alert had caused his screen to flash red — the same colour as the low-oxygen warning light he remembered from the ICU monitor — and he had found himself unable to breathe properly for nearly twenty minutes, hands gripping the edge of his keyboard, certain something was happening to him. A colleague had called building security. The incident left him shaken and, underneath that, deeply ashamed — ashamed in a way that cut closer than the earlier humiliation, because it confirmed a fear he had been carrying quietly for months: that whatever had broken in him during those eleven days in the ICU was not getting better on its own. He arrived at the intake appointment guarded and precise in his language, as though clinical accuracy might create some distance from the material. He said he was not sure therapy could help with something that felt so physical. What he was most afraid of, he admitted after a long pause, was that he would spend the rest of his life waiting for his body to betray him again. What he hoped for, more quietly, was to stop.
